It is important to include representatives from operations, engineering, laboratory, and control systems in the initial problem formulation. Problem definition should clearly define the scope of the project including (1) the expected ML response given specific process changes, (2) how the ML model will interact with the control system (i.e., direct or indirect), (3) how to assess the performance of the proposed ML system using defined, quantifiable metrics, and (4) determining the performance threshold required to merit progressing to the deployment stage after data collection, preparation, and model training. 3.2 Get Data After defining the scope of the problem, relevant data is gathered. The data comes from an array of sources in a water treatment plant: sensors and instrumentation measuring real-time quantities, chemical and biological analyses providing concentration levels, or historical maintenance logs. Data could represent measured or calculated values, or actuation data from applied commands. Each data point or observation should represent the conditions at the time the data were collected. A data collection plan that explores a wide range of operational and environmental conditions is essential because the outcomes of ML models are limited to the data used to train them. This may include additional sampling at underrepresented times of day (e.g., afternoon and evening), changes to setpoints (e.g., extreme high and low values), or wet weather events. 3.3 Prepare Data During and after data collection, raw data must be analyzed and processed to best represent the treatment process for the ML model. In the context of process engineering, this may involve removing outliers, imputing infrequently collected or missing values, or identifying important (or not important) variables or features. In computer science and statistics, a feature is a general term for a model input. It may be identical or distinct from the original, measured process variable, depending on if a data transformation has occurred. For example, using a statistical method like principal component analysis (PCA) will generate new “variables" but as these are transformed versions of original data are no longer variables in the conventional engineering sense. Hence, you often see the terms used interchangeably for the purposes of modeling treatment processes. A short list of data preparation methods explored in this work can be found in Table 2-1. Not all data analysis methods will accurately represent a process or data availability; thus, this step demands a keen eye for the nuances of both data science and water process operations to produce a clean, accurate, and comprehensive dataset for model training. Manually removing outliers is accurate but time consuming and not practical for real-time systems.
